# Focus Detection Device

The focus detection device incorporates a plurality of micro-lenses arranged in a two-dimensional array pattern. Light fluxes originating from an image forming optical system enter the device through these micro-lenses, which serve as the primary optical interface for the incoming light.

Positioned in correspondence to each of the micro-lenses are multiple light receiving elements. These elements are configured to capture the light that passes through their respective micro-lenses, enabling the device to gather detailed optical information across the entire array.

The device further includes a focus detection unit, which determines the defocus quantity of the image forming optical system. This determination is accomplished by detecting the phase difference between light fluxes that pass through different areas of the optical system, providing a precise measure of the focus state.

In addition, a recognition unit is provided to identify the characteristics of the subject image formed onto the light receiving elements. This identification is performed based on the outputs generated by the light receiving elements, allowing the device to analyze the nature of the subject being captured.

Notably, the focus detection unit optimizes its detection method for the defocus quantity in accordance with the subject image characteristics recognized by the recognition unit. By adapting its detection approach to the specific attributes of the subject image, the device achieves enhanced accuracy and reliability in focus detection across a variety of imaging conditions.

# Focus Detection Device with Adaptive Detection Based on Subject Recognition

## Overview

The present invention relates to a focus detection device designed to accurately determine the focus condition of an image forming optical system. The device employs a sophisticated arrangement that combines phase-difference detection technology with intelligent subject recognition to optimize focusing performance across a wide range of imaging scenarios.

## Structural Configuration

At the core of the device is a two-dimensional array of micro-lenses arranged in a grid pattern. Each micro-lens in this array corresponds to one or more light receiving elements, forming a densely packed detection surface. This configuration allows the device to capture spatial information across the entire image field rather than being limited to isolated detection points.

## Phase-Difference Detection Method

The device detects the defocus quantity of the image forming optical system through the principle of phase-difference detection. As light passes through the imaging optics, it traverses different optical areas—typically corresponding to separate portions of the exit pupil. The light fluxes from these distinct areas are directed onto the light receiving elements via the micro-lens array.

By measuring the phase difference between the light fluxes that have passed through these different optical areas, the device can calculate both the magnitude and direction of defocus. This information enables the system to determine precisely how far the lens must be adjusted, and in which direction, to bring the subject into sharp focus.

## Subject Recognition Function

A distinguishing feature of this device is its recognition unit, which analyzes the outputs from the same light receiving elements used for focus detection. Rather than requiring a separate sensor or optical path, the recognition unit processes the existing signal data to identify characteristics of the subject image.

These recognized characteristics may include the type of subject (such as a face, an object, or a background element), the size and position of the subject within the frame, the contrast and pattern of the subject, and other distinguishing features relevant to focusing performance.

## Adaptive Focus Detection

The principal advantage of this arrangement lies in its adaptive capability. Based on the characteristics identified by the recognition unit, the device dynamically adjusts its defocus detection method to suit the specific subject being imaged.

For example, when the recognition unit identifies a low-contrast subject, the device may modify its detection parameters to improve reliability under challenging conditions. Conversely, when a high-contrast or clearly defined subject is recognized, the device may employ a detection method optimized for speed and precision. Similarly, the detection approach may be tailored according to whether the subject is a moving object, a human face, or a stationary scene element.

## Advantages and Effect

By adapting the defocus detection method to the recognized subject image characteristics, the device consistently achieves optimal focus detection performance. This intelligent adaptation ensures that focusing accuracy and speed are maintained even as imaging conditions vary—whether due to changes in lighting, subject type, movement, or scene composition.

As a result, the focus detection device provides reliable and precise autofocus performance tailored to each unique imaging situation, overcoming the limitations of conventional systems that rely on a single, fixed detection method regardless of subject characteristics.
outputs.L5:
# Focus Detection

Focus detection is a fundamental technology used in optical systems, particularly in cameras and imaging devices, to determine whether a subject is sharply captured or appears blurred. This capability forms the backbone of modern autofocus systems, enabling both professional photographers and casual users to achieve crisp, well-defined images with minimal effort.

## How Focus Detection Works

At its core, focus detection measures the sharpness or clarity of light rays converging at the image sensor. When a subject is perfectly in focus, light from a single point converges precisely on the sensor plane. When out of focus, the light spreads out, creating a blurred appearance. Detection systems analyze these differences to make adjustments automatically.

There are two primary methods used in most devices:

**Phase Detection Autofocus (PDAF)**
This method splits incoming light into two separate images and compares them. By measuring the "phase difference" between these images, the system can quickly determine both the direction and amount of adjustment needed. Phase detection is fast and highly effective, making it popular in DSLR cameras and modern smartphones for tracking moving subjects.

**Contrast Detection Autofocus**
This approach analyzes the contrast between adjacent pixels in the image. Maximum contrast typically indicates optimal focus, as sharp edges create the greatest differences in brightness. While slightly slower than phase detection, contrast detection is often more accurate and works well in live-view and video applications.

## Applications

Focus detection extends beyond consumer photography. It plays a critical role in:

- **Microscopy**, where precise focus is essential for scientific observation
- **Machine vision** systems used in manufacturing and quality control
- **Medical imaging** devices that require exceptional clarity
- **Surveillance and security** equipment for capturing clear footage

## Conclusion

Focus detection represents an essential intersection of optics, electronics, and software. As technology advances, hybrid systems combining multiple detection methods continue to improve speed and accuracy, ensuring that capturing sharp images becomes increasingly effortless across a wide range of devices and industries.

# Patent Claim: Focus Detection Device

**Claim 1.** A focus detection device comprising:

a plurality of microlenses arranged in a two-dimensional array;

a plurality of light receiving elements disposed corresponding to each of said microlenses, each of said microlenses directing incident light from a subject onto a respective pair of said light receiving elements, wherein a first light receiving element of said pair receives a first light flux passing through a first pupil region of an imaging optical system and a second light receiving element of said pair receives a second light flux passing through a second pupil region of said imaging optical system;

a signal generator configured to generate a first image signal from output of said first light receiving elements and a second image signal from output of said second light receiving elements;

a phase difference calculator configured to calculate a relative phase difference between said first image signal and said second image signal;

a subject image characteristic analyzer configured to determine a characteristic value of a subject image based on at least one of a spatial frequency component, a contrast distribution, and an edge intensity of at least one of said first image signal and said second image signal; and

a defocus calculator configured to compute a defocus amount and a defocus direction based on said relative phase difference calculated by said phase difference calculator, wherein said defocus calculator adjusts said computed defocus amount according to said characteristic value determined by said subject image characteristic analyzer.

---

**Claim 2.** The focus detection device according to claim 1, wherein said subject image characteristic analyzer is further configured to determine a reliability value of said relative phase difference based on said characteristic value, and said defocus calculator selectively computes said defocus amount when said reliability value exceeds a predetermined threshold.

**Claim 3.** The focus detection device according to claim 1, wherein said defocus calculator applies a correction coefficient to said relative phase difference, said correction coefficient being determined as a function of said spatial frequency component of said subject image.

**Claim 4.** The focus detection device according to claim 1, further comprising a memory storing a plurality of conversion coefficients each associated with a respective range of said characteristic value, wherein said defocus calculator selects one of said conversion coefficients based on said determined characteristic value and converts said relative phase difference into said defocus amount using said selected conversion coefficient.

---

*Note: This is a sample claim drafted for illustrative purposes. An actual patent application should be prepared or reviewed by a registered patent attorney or agent, and claims should be tailored to the specific novel features of the invention and drafted in view of prior art to ensure patentability and appropriate scope.*

**Claim 1.**

A focus detection apparatus for an optical imaging system, comprising:

a plurality of micro-lenses arranged in a two-dimensional array and disposed adjacent to an imaging plane of the optical imaging system, each micro-lens being configured to receive a luminous flux from an imaging optical system and to divide said luminous flux into a plurality of partial luminous fluxes corresponding to different pupil regions of the imaging optical system;

a plurality of light receiving elements disposed in correspondence with each of said plurality of micro-lenses, each of said light receiving elements being positioned to receive a respective one of said partial luminous fluxes and to output an electrical signal representing an intensity of the received partial luminous flux;

a focus detection unit operatively coupled to said plurality of light receiving elements, said focus detection unit being configured to detect a focus state of the optical imaging system by determining a phase difference between a pair of image signals generated from the electrical signals output by light receiving elements corresponding to mutually different pupil regions, and to compute a defocus amount based on said phase difference; and

*Dependent claims (illustrative):*

**Claim 2.** The focus detection apparatus according to claim 1, wherein said recognition unit is configured to identify a predetermined feature of the subject and to preferentially select the focus detection region corresponding to a position of said identified feature.

**Claim 3.** The focus detection apparatus according to claim 1, further comprising a control unit configured to drive a focusing lens of the imaging optical system in accordance with the defocus amount computed by said focus detection unit.

**Claim 4.** The focus detection apparatus according to claim 1, wherein each of said light receiving elements is a photoelectric conversion element formed on a common image sensor substrate, and said plurality of micro-lenses is integrally formed over said image sensor substrate.
